title: Hook Best Practices
description: Follow best practices for hook design, naming, composition, and documentation.

data.text: Hooks are the building blocks of React's component model. Writing them well means understanding the rules of hooks, designing for composability, naming for discoverability, and documenting behavior so other developers can use them correctly.

data.title: Two Ironclad Rules
data.text: Only call hooks at the top level. Do not call them inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.

React relies on the order in which hooks are called to associate state with the correct hook. Conditional or looped calls change that order between renders, corrupting state. The ESLint plugin `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` enforces these rules at build time.

data.title: Incorrect: Hook Inside Condition
data.content: This violates the rules of hooks and will break state.

data.title: Correct: Move Condition Inside Hook
data.content: Keep hooks at the top level; put conditions inside them.

data.text: Custom hooks should start with `use` so developers and tooling recognize them immediately. The name should describe the behavior, not the implementation. Prefer `useLocalStorage` over `useStorageWithJSONAndSSRHandling`.

Small, single-purpose hooks compose naturally. A `useMouse` hook that returns coordinates pairs well with a `useDrag` hook that consumes them. Avoid mega-hooks that bundle unrelated concerns—they are harder to test, harder to optimize, and harder to reuse.

data.title: Composing Small Hooks
data.content: Build a draggable component by composing useMouse and useState.

data.title: Extract When You Repeat
data.text: If three components share the same useEffect or state logic, extract it into a custom hook. If only one component uses it, keep it inline.

Document inputs, outputs, and edge cases. Use TypeScript to make the contract explicit, and provide JSDoc for consumers who rely on IntelliSense. Note whether the hook is strict about dependencies, whether it cleans up after itself, and whether it supports SSR.

data.title: Well-Documented Hook Signature
data.content: TypeScript types and JSDoc describe the full API.

items.text: Name starts with 'use' and describes behavior
All hooks called unconditionally at the top level
items.hint: No loops, conditions, or nested functions around hooks

items.text: Dependencies arrays are exhaustive and minimal

items.hint: Return a cleanup function from useEffect when subscribing

items.text: Types are exported for consumer inference
items.hint: Avoid 'as any' and internal-only shapes in the public API

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Hooks must always be called in the same order on every render.
Compose small, focused hooks rather than building large monolithic ones.
Name hooks for behavior, not implementation details.
Document contracts with TypeScript types and JSDoc comments.
Always clean up subscriptions, timers, and event listeners.
data.takeaway: Great hooks feel like native React features: predictable, composable, and well-documented.
